recentItems.title: Moroccan Unique Rr51 at the Hot Summer BUG Match
recentItems.description:
It's pretty hot out here in the southern Arizona summer, so I figured I'd lean into it. For the BUG Match this month, I have an-Moroccan police Unique Rr51. This is a simple blowback .32 ACP pistol made by MAPH in a bunch of variations for many decades. It holds 9 rounds in the magazine, and I've paired it with a vaguely North African Foreign Legion set of kit just for fun.

Ultimately, the match went amazingly well until that last stage. My 9 rounds was not enough to complete the course of fire there, and it was worth so many points that it outweighed all the other stages. Ah well...

recentItems.title: 1789 Girardoni Air Rifle: A Generation Ahead of Its Time
recentItems.description:
Designed by Bartolomeo Girardoni the in the 1770s, the Girardoni is an air rifle that can fire 20 rounds as quickly as a modern bolt action rifle. It uses .46 caliber round lead balls, delivering 154 grains of lead per shot at about 1000 fps. This was a revolutionary weapon when it was created, and it was adopted by the Austrian army. However, its manufacturing was very difficult, and not enough were made before the inventor's death to make a significant effect on and battles. Poor tactical use of the guns that did get into service didn't help. It wasn't until more than 60 years later that an equally effective military rifle was developed, that being the Spencer.

recentItems.title: ARAC: Making Submachine Guns from Bolt Actions
recentItems.description:
In 1954 and 1955, the French company SOFAM (Société de Fabrication d'Armaments) in Paris marketed a system to convert bolt action rifles into submachine guns. The original design is reportedly Spanish, but was marketed through the French company. The design was pretty simple, using the stock and trigger guard of the rifle (in these examples a Mauser 98, but conceivably any type would do) and manufacturing a new receiver, bolt, barrel, and trigger system to go with them. The pitch was that production could be stood up in six months with minimal technological outlay, ideal for less-developed nations looking to upgrade their small arms. However, the cost calculations didn't appear to make sense, as no buyers were found.

Many thanks to the IRCGN (Institut de Recherche Criminelle de la Gendarmerie Nationale) for allowing me access to film these two examples for you!

recentItems.title: Aimpoint's 3.5x Scope for French Trials
recentItems.description:
Aimpoint is known for its red dot optics, but in the early 2000s the company decided to develop a 3.5x fixed magnification traditional scope. It was intended for a French military trial, and Aimpoint used their 3x magnifier as the base for building it. I have three different iterations of the project to show, none of which ended up winning the contract.

recentItems.title: Saco Defense M683: A Super-Simple SMG for the US Army
recentItems.description:
During the 1980s, the US ran the Joint Service Small Arms Program to reduce the number of different small arms in US inventory. The most significant outcome of this program was the M9 pistol, but the program also considered adopting a submachine gun. The requirements were bit tricky, with things like a low rate of fire but also a very high-ROF burst option, and caliber conversion options. Saco Defense got its hands on a Brazilian Uru submachine gun and used it as a model for their Model 683 for this program. Only a few were made, and we are taking a look at them today...

Thanks to the Institute of Military Technology for allowing me to have access to these prototypes and bring them to you! Check them out at:
http://www.instmiltech.com
